## Appendix A Conjugacy of the DAG-BLR prior

We begin by remarking on the relationship between the DAG-BLR prior and the well-studied DAG-Wishart prior.

#### Remark 1.

The DAG-BLR prior is a generalization of the (multi-shape) DAG-Wishart prior introduced in [10] and used in later works including [16]. In particular, as mentioned in Section 3.1 of [16], the DAG-Wishart prior with parameters $U$ and $\tilde{\alpha}$ , for $U\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}$ positive definite, is a special case of the prior used in this work with

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{i} \displaystyle=\frac{\tilde{\alpha}_{i}}{2}-\frac{|\pa(i)|}{2}-1, \displaystyle\beta_{i} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(U_{ii}-U_{i,\pa(i)}U_{\pa(i),\pa(i)}^{-1}U_{\pa(i),i}\right), \displaystyle{\mathbf{m}}_{i} \displaystyle=U_{\pa(i),\pa(i)}^{-1}U_{\pa(i),i}, \displaystyle{\mathbf{M}}_{i} \displaystyle=U_{\pa(i),\pa(i)}^{-1} $$

Note that, in general, the DAG-Wishart prior imposes more constraints than the DAG-BLR prior. For example, given two nodes $i$ and $j$ such that $\pa(i)=\pa(j)$ , the DAG-Wishart prior requires that ${\mathbf{M}}_{i}={\mathbf{M}}_{j}$ , i.e., the covariance over the edge weights into $i$ must be equal to the covariance over the edge weights into $j$ . These constraints ensure that the DAG-Wishart prior satisfies desirable properties for model selection such as score equivalence [65]. However, these constraints are not necessary to ensure that the DAG-BLR prior is a conjugate prior. In this paper, we do not use our prior over ${\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}$ for model selection - we only require that the prior is a conjugate prior. Thus, we present our results for the more general case.

### A.1 Conjugacy in the observational setting

Here, we prove that the DAG-BLR prior is a conjugate prior to the Gaussian likelihood, and provide equations for the posterior hyperparameters. This section applies in the observational setting without interventions, where all samples acquired follow Eq. (1) in the main text.

#### Claim 1.

Let $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})$ be a DAG-BLR distribution with hyperparameters $\{\alpha_{i},\beta_{i},{\mathbf{m}}_{i},{\mathbf{M}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{p}$ . Let $\mathcal{D}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ be sampled from a linear Gaussian DAG model with parameters $({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})$ . Then $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{D}_{t})$ is a DAG-BLR distribution with hyperparameters $\{\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\}_{i=1}^{p}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle=\alpha_{i}+\frac{n}{2}, \displaystyle\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle=\beta_{i}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{m=1}^{n}(\mathsf{x}^{(m)}_{i})^{2}+{\mathbf{m}}_{i}^{\top}{\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}{\mathbf{m}}_{i}-{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{\top}{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{-1}{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\right), \displaystyle{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle={\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}{\mathbf{m}}_{i}+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\mathsf{x}_{i}^{(m)}\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}^{(m)}\right), \displaystyle{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle=\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}^{(m)}\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}^{(m)~\top}\right)^{-1}. $$

#### Proof.

We begin by proving that $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}})=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)})$ . In particular, it holds by the DAG factorization structure on $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})$ and the product structure on $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})$ that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}}(\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2},\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)})\right) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}}\left(\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2},\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)})\right) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}). $$

Next, we prove that $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathsf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\left(\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)})\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},\mathsf{x}_{i})\right)$ . Namely:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathsf{x}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}\mid{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2})\right)\cdot\left(\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2})\right) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2})\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2}) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i},{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma^{2}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\left(\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)})\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma^{2}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},\mathsf{x}_{i})\right) $$

In the fourth line, we used the chain rule together with the independence of ${\mathbf{B}}_{i},\sigma_{i}$ from $\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}$ , and in the fifth line we used the chain rule again. Combining Eq. (19) and Eq. (20), we obtain that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathbf{x}})=\frac{\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}},{\mathbf{x}})}{\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}})}=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma^{2}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},\mathsf{x}_{i}). $$

Finally, we note that, for $\mathcal{D}_{t}=\{{\mathbf{x}}\}$ , it holds that, for $\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\bm{}i(\mathcal{D}_{t}),$ and ${\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})$ defined in Eq. (18),

$$ \mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},\mathsf{x}_{i})=\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)};{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\sigma_{i}^{2}{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}))\cdot\mathcal{I}\mathcal{G}(\sigma_{i}^{2};\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})) $$

by standard results on the conjugacy of the normal-inverse-gamma distribution for Bayesian linear regression (e.g., Proposition 2.11 of [39]). The result for the case of general $n$ follows by induction, which completes the proof. ∎

### A.2 Conjugacy in the setting of shift interventions with known values

Next, we extend the previous section by considering the interventional setting with known shift interventions. In particular, we present the proof of Lemma 1 in the main text, which we restate here for ease of reading and also specify the hyperparameter updates.

#### Lemma 1.

The posterior corresponding to the DAG-BLR prior satisfies $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{D}_{t})=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2}|\mathcal{D}_{t})$ , where $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2}|\mathcal{D}_{t})$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{i}^{2}|\mathcal{D}_{t} \displaystyle\sim\mathcal{I}\mathcal{G}\big(\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\big), \displaystyle{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)}|\sigma_{i}^{2},\mathcal{D}_{t} \displaystyle\sim\mathcal{N}\big({\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\sigma_{i}^{2}{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\big), $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle=\alpha_{i}+\frac{n}{2}, \displaystyle\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle=\beta_{i}+\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{m=1}^{n}(\mathsf{x}^{(m)}_{i}-a_{i}^{(m)})^{2}+{\mathbf{m}}_{i}^{\top}{\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}{\mathbf{m}}_{i}-{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{\top}{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{-1}{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\right), \displaystyle{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle={\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}{\mathbf{m}}_{i}+\sum_{m=1}^{n}(\mathsf{x}_{i}^{(m)}-a_{i}^{(m)})\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}^{(m)}\right), \displaystyle{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle=\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}+\sum_{m=1}^{n}\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}^{(m)}\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}^{(m)~\top}\right)^{-1}. $$

#### Proof.

Note that, by the definition of a shift intervention,

$$ \mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}};{\mathbf{a}})=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}\left(\mathsf{x}_{i}^{(m)}-a_{i}^{(m)}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}\right). $$

Thus, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}};{\mathbf{a}}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}}(\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}};{\mathbf{a}})) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i}\mid{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2},\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)})\right) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}}\left(\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i}\mid{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2},\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)})\right) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{\pa(i)}). $$

Similarly, we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}},{\mathbf{x}};{\mathbf{a}}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}}\mid{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}};{\mathbf{a}})\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2})\right)\cdot\left(\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2})\right) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2})\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2}) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i},{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma^{2}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)}) \displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\left(\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)})\cdot\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma^{2}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i})\right). $$

Then by combining Eq. (22) and Eq. (23), we obtain that

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathbf{x}})=\frac{\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}},{\mathbf{x}})}{\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}})}=\prod_{i=1}^{p}\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma^{2}_{i}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i}). $$

Once again, by conjugacy of the normal-inverse Gamma distribution for Bayesian linear regression, we have

$$ \mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)},\sigma_{i}^{2}\mid\mathsf{x}_{\pa(i)},\mathsf{x}_{i}-a_{i})=\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)};{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\sigma_{i}^{2}{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}))\cdot\mathcal{I}\mathcal{G}(\sigma_{i}^{2};\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})) $$

for $\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\bm{}i(\mathcal{D}_{t}),$ and ${\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})$ defined in Eq. (21), which concludes the proof. ∎

#### Remark 2.

Note that Lemma 1 can easily be extended to hard interventions by updating only the hyperparameters indexed by nodes $i$ that are not an interventional target.

## Appendix B Details for Causal Integrated Variance

In this section, we show how to evaluate the CIV acquisition function in closed form. This then allows for the use of gradient-based optimization methods. Recall that the causal integrated variance (CIV) acquisition function is defined as

$$ h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}}), $$

where $g({\mathbf{a}})=\|({\mathbf{a}}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{m=1}^{n}{\bm{\epsilon}}_{n})-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})=\mathcal{D}_{t}\cup(\bar{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\prime}_{[n]},{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ with $\bar{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\prime}_{[n]}$ being $n$ repetitions of $\bar{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\prime}=({\mathbf{I}}-\mathbb{E}({\mathbf{B}}|\mathcal{D}_{t}))^{-1}{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ .

We remark here that if only a subset of variables $S$ are of interest in the target mean ${\bm{\mu}}^{*}$ , we can replace $g({\mathbf{a}})$ with a projected version $g({\mathbf{a}})=\min_{[{\bm{\mu}}]_{S}=[{\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{S}}\|({\mathbf{a}}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{m=1}^{n}{\bm{\epsilon}}^{(m)})-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}\|_{2}^{2}$ that measures the discrepancy only over the variables in $S$ . This minimization problem can be solved exactly by writing ${\bm{\mu}}={\bm{\mu}}^{*}+\mathbf{P}_{S}{\mathbf{v}}$ where $\mathbf{P}_{S}$ is a projection matrix that sets the $S$ -entries of ${\mathbf{v}}$ to zero. Solving for ${\mathbf{v}}$ results in $g({\mathbf{a}})=\|({\mathbf{a}}+\frac{1}{n}\sum_{m=1}^{n}{\bm{\epsilon}}^{(m)})-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}\|_{\mathbf{Q}_{S}}^{2}$ , where $\mathbf{Q}_{S}={\mathbf{I}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}})\mathbf{P}_{S}(({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}})\mathbf{P}_{S})^{\dagger}$ . To evaluate and optimize CIV, we could for example use a plug-in estimand for $\mathbf{Q}_{S}$ and follow similar derivations as below.

For minimizing (or maximizing) the values of a subset of nodes $S$ , we can modify the optimality gap to be a scalar objective function that describes how well the subset of nodes is optimized (e.g., $g({\mathbf{a}})=\max_{i\in S}{\bm{\mu}}^{*}_{i}=\max_{i\in S}[({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}})^{-1}{\mathbf{a}}]_{i}$ for minimization). However, since the variance of this function may not be computable in closed form, approximation methods may need to be developed to evaluate and optimize CIV in this case.

### B.1 Evaluations

We first show how to evaluate the term inside the integral, $\sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}^{2}$ , which characterizes the post- ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ uncertainty of estimating the optimality of intervention ${\mathbf{a}}$ . To this end, we will need the following lemma on the hyperparameters of the DAG-BLR distribution.

#### Lemma 2.

Given the current dataset $\mathcal{D}_{t}$ and the augmented dataset $\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ , the posterior updates on the hyperparameters $\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})),\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))$ and ${\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))$ do not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ . In particular, $\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))=\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+\frac{n}{2}$ , whereas $\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))=\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})$ and ${\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))={\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{i})$ .

#### Proof.

First, by Lemma 1., it holds that $\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))=\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+\frac{n}{2}$ . Second, it holds that

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbf{m}}_{i}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big) \displaystyle=\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{-1}+n\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{\pa(i)}\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\prime\top}\right)^{-1}\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}(\mathcal{D}_{t}){\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+n(\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{i}-a^{\prime}_{i})\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}\right) \displaystyle=\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{-1}+n\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{\pa(i)}\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\prime\top}\right)^{-1}\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}(\mathcal{D}_{t}){\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+n\big(\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\prime\top}{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\big)\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{\pa(i)}\right) \displaystyle=\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{-1}+n\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{\pa(i)}\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\prime\top}\right)^{-1}\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}(\mathcal{D}_{t}){\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+n\big(\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{\pa(i)}\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\prime\top}\big){\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\right) \displaystyle={\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}), $$

where we used $\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}-a^{\prime}_{i}=\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\prime\top}{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})$ in the second equation. Lastly, it follows that,

$$ \displaystyle\beta_{i}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big) \displaystyle=\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\Big[n(\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}-a^{\prime}_{i})^{2}+{\mathbf{m}}_{i}^{\top}(\mathcal{D}_{t}){\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}(\mathcal{D}_{t}){\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})-{\mathbf{m}}_{i}^{\top}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big){\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big){\mathbf{m}}_{i}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)\Big] \displaystyle=\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\Big[n(\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}-a^{\prime}_{i})^{2}+{\mathbf{m}}_{i}^{\top}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\Big({\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}(\mathcal{D}_{t})-{\mathbf{M}}_{i}^{-1}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)\Big){\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\Big] \displaystyle=\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+\frac{1}{2}\big[n(\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{i}-a^{\prime}_{i})^{2}-{\mathbf{m}}_{i}^{\top}(\mathcal{D}_{t})(n\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\prime}\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\prime\top}){\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\big] \displaystyle=\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}). $$

Therefore, the updates for these three variables do not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ , which completes the proof. ∎

With this result, we can now calculate $\sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}^{2}$ by proving a generalized version of Proposition 1 from the main text in which we do not condition on a known ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ . The major techniques we will employ are the law of total expectation and variance. These allow us to separate various sources of randomness and obtain a closed-form expression.

#### Remark 3.

For convenience, we record the mean and variance (or moments) for a number of distributions which will be used in the following proof. First, suppose $W\sim(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}))^{2}$ . Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}(W) \displaystyle=\sigma^{2}+\mu^{2}, \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(W) \displaystyle=2\sigma^{4}+4\mu^{2}\sigma^{2}. $$

Next, suppose $W\sim\mathcal{I}\mathcal{G}(\alpha,\beta)$ . Then for $k\in\mathbb{N}_{+}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}(W^{k}) \displaystyle=\frac{\beta^{k}\Gamma(\alpha-k)}{\Gamma(\alpha)}=\frac{\beta^{k}}{(\alpha-1)...(\alpha-k)}. $$

Finally, suppose $W\sim\bar{\chi}^{2}({\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{k}},{\bm{\lambda}},0,0)$ , where $\bar{\chi}^{2}$ denotes a generalized chi-square distribution [23]. Then

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}(W) \displaystyle=\sum_{j}w_{j}(k_{j}+\lambda_{j}), \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}(W) \displaystyle=2\sum_{j}w_{j}^{2}(k_{j}+2\lambda_{j}). $$

#### Proposition 1.

The variance $\sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}^{2}$ satisfies

$$ \sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}^{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+4u_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\right]+c, $$

where only $u_{i}:={\bm{\mu}}_{\pa(i)}^{*\top}{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})){\bm{\mu}}_{\pa(i)}^{*}$ depends on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ . The variables $\alpha_{i}^{\prime}:=\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+\frac{n}{2}$ , $\beta_{i}^{\prime}:=\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})$ and $b_{i}:={\bm{\mu}}_{i}^{*}-{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{\top}{\bm{\mu}}_{\pa(i)}^{*}$ only depend on $\mathcal{D}_{t}$ . The scalar $c$ is a constant that does not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ .

#### Proof.

First, note that the uncertainty in $\sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}^{2}$ comes from two sources: ${\mathbf{B}}$ and ${\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]}$ , which jointly depend on ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ . By the law of total variance, we condition out ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}^{2} \displaystyle=\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]},{\mathbf{B}}}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big) \displaystyle=\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}}\Big(\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]},{\mathbf{B}}}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)\Big|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\Big)+\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}}\Big(\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]},{\mathbf{B}}}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)\Big|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\Big). $$

Now, we evaluate the inside terms conditioning on ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ using another layer of the law of total expectation and variance:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]},{\mathbf{B}}}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}}}\big(\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]}}(g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}}}\big(\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]}}(g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big), \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]},{\mathbf{B}}}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}_{{\mathbf{B}}}\big(\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]}}(g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}}}\big(\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]}}(g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}_{{\mathbf{B}}}\big(\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]}}(g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{B}}}\big(\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]}}(g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big), $$

where we used the fact that $g({\mathbf{a}})$ is independent of $\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ conditioning on ${\mathbf{B}}$ and ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ . Conditioning on ${\mathbf{B}}$ and ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ , we can see that the random variable

$$ g({\mathbf{a}})=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{m=1}^{n}{\bm{\epsilon}}_{m}\right]_{i}+[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}\right)^{2} $$

is a sum of squares of $p$ independent Gaussian variables $[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{m=1}^{n}{\bm{\epsilon}}_{m}]_{i}+[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}([{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i},\frac{1}{n}\sigma_{i}^{2})$ , and therefore follows a generalized chi-square distribution

$$ g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}\sim\bar{\chi}^{2}\left(\frac{1}{n}\diag({\bm{\Sigma}}),\mathbf{1},{\bm{\lambda}},0,0\right), $$

where ${\bm{\lambda}}=n\diag({\bm{\Sigma}}^{-1}[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}][{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]^{\top})$ and notation $\diag(\cdot)$ denotes the diagonal vector of a matrix. Thus, by Eq. (26), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]}}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}\big) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{n}+[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}^{2}\right), \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]}}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}\big) \displaystyle=2\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{4}}{n^{2}}+\frac{2\sigma_{i}^{2}}{n}[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}^{2}\right). $$

Then, conditioning the right-hand sides on ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ and $\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ , we obtain by Lemma 1 that the only variable terms are $[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}^{2}=(a_{i}-\mu_{i}^{*}+{\bm{\mu}}^{*\top}_{\pa(i)}{\mathbf{B}}_{i,\pa(i)})^{2}\sim\mathcal{N}(a_{i}-b_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2}u_{i})^{2}$ , which are independent among different $i\in[p]$ . Therefore, by Eq. (28), Eq. (29), and Eq. (24), we have

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]},{\mathbf{B}}}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{B}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{n}+[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}^{2}\right)\bigg|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\right) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{n}+\sigma_{i}^{2}u_{i}+(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\right), \displaystyle\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\epsilon}}_{[n]},{\mathbf{B}}}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big) \displaystyle=\mathrm{Var}_{\mathbf{B}}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{n}+[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}^{2}\right)\bigg|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\right) \displaystyle+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{B}}\left(2\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{4}}{n^{2}}+\frac{2\sigma_{i}^{2}}{n}[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}^{2}\right)\bigg|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\right) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left[\mathrm{Var}_{\mathbf{B}}\big([{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}^{2}\big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)+2\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{B}}\left(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{4}}{n^{2}}+\frac{2\sigma_{i}^{2}}{n}[{\mathbf{a}}-({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}]_{i}^{2}\Big|{\bm{\Sigma}},\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\right)\right] \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left[\big(2\sigma_{i}^{4}u_{i}^{2}+4\sigma_{i}^{2}u_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\big)+2\Big(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{4}}{n^{2}}+\frac{2\sigma_{i}^{2}}{n}\big(\sigma_{i}^{2}u_{i}+(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\big)\Big)\right] \displaystyle=2\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left[\sigma_{i}^{4}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+2\sigma_{i}^{2}u_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\right]+c_{1}, $$

where $c_{1}=2\sum_{i=1}^{p}(\nicefrac{{\sigma_{i}^{4}}}{{n^{2}}}+2\nicefrac{{\sigma_{i}^{2}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}}}{{n}})$ is a scalar that only depends on ${\bm{\Sigma}},{\mathbf{a}}$ and ${\mathbf{b}}$ .

Next, we calculate $\sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}^{2}$ . Using Lemma 1 and Lemma 2, we know that conditioning on $\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ , the random variable $\sigma_{i}^{2}$ follows an inverse Gamma distribution with hyperparameters $\alpha^{\prime}_{i}$ and $\beta^{\prime}_{i}$ . Since $\alpha^{\prime}_{i}$ and $\beta^{\prime}_{i}$ do not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ , we then know that the distribution of ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ conditioned on $\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ does not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ . In turn, conditioning on $\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ , $c_{1}$ in Eq. (30), which only depends on ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ , ${\mathbf{a}}$ and ${\mathbf{b}}$ , does not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ . Thus, using Eq. (30) in Eq. (27) and then Eq. (25), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle~~~~\sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}^{2} \displaystyle=\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\big(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{2}}{n}+\sigma_{i}^{2}u_{i}+(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\big)\Big|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\Big)+\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}}\Big(2\sum_{i=1}^{p}\big[\sigma_{i}^{4}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+2\sigma_{i}^{2}u_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\big]+c_{1}\Big|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\Big) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\mathrm{Var}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}(\sigma_{i}^{2})\left(u_{i}+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{2}+2\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left[\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}(\sigma_{i}^{4})\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+2\mathbb{E}_{{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}(\sigma_{i}^{2})u_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\right]+c_{1} \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{(\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}\left(u_{i}+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{2}+\frac{2\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+4u_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\right]+c_{1} \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+4u_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\right]+c, $$

where $c$ is constant that does not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ , thereby completing the proof. ∎

Conditioning on ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ in the above result gives rise to the following corollary, which is Proposition 1 in the main text. The calculation is similar to the case of unknown ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ , but simplifies since we do not need to consider the randomness in ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ anymore.

#### Corollary 1.

Conditioning on ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ , the variance $\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}=2\sum_{i=1}^{p}\big(v_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}v_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}+2v_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\big)+c, $$

where only $v_{i}:=\sigma_{i}^{2}{\bm{\mu}}^{*\top}_{\pa(i)}{\mathbf{M}}_{i}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big){\bm{\mu}}_{\pa(i)}^{*}$ depends on the augmented dataset $\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ ; the variable $b_{i}:=\mu_{i}^{*}-{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{\top}{\bm{\mu}}^{*}_{\pa(i)}$ and constant $c$ do not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ .

#### Proof.

From Eq. (27) and Eq. (30), we know that conditioning on ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ results in

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})} \displaystyle=2\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left[\sigma_{i}^{4}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+2\sigma_{i}^{2}u_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\right]+c_{1} \displaystyle=2\sum_{i=1}^{p}\left(v_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}v_{i}\sigma_{i}^{2}+2v_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\right)+c_{1}, $$

where $c=c_{1}$ does not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ , thereby completing the proof. ∎

Next, we show in the following lemma that, for any ${\mathbf{a}}\in\mathcal{A}$ , we can trivially make the uncertainty $\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}$ smaller by increasing the magnitude of ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ . This has previously been observed in the Bayesian linear regression setting [70]. To show this result formally for our problem, we need the above closed-form results and the posterior of the DAG-BLR distribution.

#### Lemma 3.

For any $r>1$ , there is

$$ \sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}(r{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}\leq\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}. $$

#### Proof.

Using Proposition 1., since only $u_{i}$ depends on the augmented dataset $\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ and $\mathcal{D}_{t}(r{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ , we can show that $\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}(r{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}\leq\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}$ by showing $u_{i}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}(r{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)\leq u_{i}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)$ . This follows directly from

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbf{M}}_{i}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}(r{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)=\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{-1}+nr^{2}\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\top}\right)^{-1}\preceq\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{-1}+n\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\top}\right)^{-1}={\mathbf{M}}_{i}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big), $$

which completes the proof. ∎

Therefore, we set $\mathcal{A}$ to be the unit hypersphere $\mathbb{S}^{p-1}=\{{\mathbf{a}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\|{\mathbf{a}}\|_{2}=1\}$ and only optimize over the direction of an intervention and not its magnitude. When $\nu$ is the uniform measure on $\mathcal{A}$ , we can calculate $h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ analytically. The following proposition provides the explicit form, which is a generalized version of Proposition 2 in the main text.

#### Proposition 2.

For $\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ and $\nu$ being the uniform measure on $\mathcal{A}$ , the CIV acquisition function evaluated at ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+4u_{i}\left(b_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{p}\right)\right]+C, $$

where $C$ is a constant that does not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ .

#### Proof.

Using Proposition 1., we obtain that

$$ \displaystyle h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-1}}\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}d\nu({\mathbf{a}}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-1}}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+4u_{i}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}\right]+c\right\}d\nu({\mathbf{a}}) \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+4u_{i}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-1}}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})\right]+C \displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+4u_{i}\left(b_{i}^{2}+\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-1}}(a_{i}^{2}-2a_{i}b_{i})d\nu({\mathbf{a}})\right)\right]+C, $$

where $C$ is a constant that does not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ . Since $\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ is symmetric and isometric, we have

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-1}}a_{i}b_{i}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})=b_{i}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-1}}a_{i}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})=0, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-1}}a_{i}^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-1}}a_{i}^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})=\frac{1}{p}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-1}}\|{\mathbf{a}}\|_{2}^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})=\frac{1}{p}. $$

Thus plugging Eq. (32) and Eq. (33) into Eq. (31), we obtain that

$$ \displaystyle h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+4u_{i}\left(b_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{p}\right)\right]+C, $$

which completes the proof. ∎

To obtain the simpler version provided in the main text as Proposition 2 where ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ is fixed, we can use a similar calculation following the same simplifications as in Corollary 1.

These closed-form expressions also provide a way to save computation computational costs when evaluating the acquisition function for multiple ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ . Since $\alpha_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})),\beta_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))$ , and ${\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))$ do not depend on the value of ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ , they can be calculated once and saved for evaluating different ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ . The only variable in $h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ that depends on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ , which needs to be calculated for each point, is $u_{i}$ (which depends on ${\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))$ ). This is because

$$ \displaystyle{\mathbf{M}}_{i}\big(\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)=\left({\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{-1}+n\bar{\mathsf{x}}^{\prime}_{\pa(i)}\bar{\mathsf{x}}_{\pa(i)}^{\prime\top}\right)^{-1}, $$

where $\bar{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}=({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{m}}(\mathcal{D}_{t}))^{-1}{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ and ${\mathbf{m}}(\mathcal{D}_{t}):=\mathbb{E}({\mathbf{B}}|\mathcal{D}_{t})$ is a $p$ -by- $p$ matrix consisting of the current estimates of the edge weights of the underlying graph, i.e., its entries are $[{\mathbf{m}}(\mathcal{D}_{t})]_{i,\pa(i)}={\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})^{\top}$ for all $i\in[p]$ and $[{\mathbf{m}}(\mathcal{D}_{t})]_{i,k}=0$ for all $i\in[p],~k\notin\pa(i)$ . Thus, we can evaluate $h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ for each ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}$ efficiently using the updated hyperparameters $\{\alpha(\mathcal{D}_{t}),\beta(\mathcal{D}_{t}),{\mathbf{m}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t}),{\mathbf{M}}_{i}(\mathcal{D}_{t})\}_{i=1}^{p}$ . The computational complexity of evaluating CIV for a single ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ is $O(p^{3})$ .

### B.2 Optimization

When optimizing $h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ on $\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ , we can relax the constraint to the unit ball $\mathbb{B}^{p}=\{{\mathbf{a}}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:\|{\mathbf{a}}\|_{2}\leq 1\}$ (which is convex). This is a consequence of Lemma 3, which shows that for all ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{B}^{p}$ , it holds that $h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})\geq h(\frac{{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}}{\|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}\|_{2}},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ . Therefore minimizing $h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ over $\mathbb{B}^{p}$ will always return points on $\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ . In other words, we solve for ${\mathbf{a}}^{(t+1)}$ by

$$ \min_{{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{B}^{p}}h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t}),\quad s.t.~\|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}\|_{2}\leq 1. $$

The particular optimizers used for solving this problem are given in Methods in the main text. We summarize the entire procedure in Algorithm 1.

```
causal graph $\mathcal{G}$ , samples $\mathcal{D}$ , target mean ${\bm{\mu}}^{*}$
initialize DAG-Wishart prior $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}})$ ;
if $\mathcal{D}$ is not empty then
update $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{D})$ as in Lemma 1.
end if
while not exceed time step limit do
select ${\mathbf{a}}={\textrm{argmin}}_{{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}}h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D})$ as in Proposition 2.
obtain samples from ${\mathbf{a}}$ and append to $\mathcal{D}$
update $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{D})$ as in Lemma 1.
end while
estimated optimal intervention $({\mathbf{I}}-\mathbb{E}({\mathbf{B}}|\mathcal{D})){\bm{\mu}}^{*}$
```

*Algorithm 1 Active Learning for Intervention Design*

## Appendix C Details for Causal Output-weighted Integrated Variance

### C.1 Background on Output-weighted Integrated Variance

When studying sequential sampling for the purpose of estimating linear mappings between inputs and outputs, [22] proposed to use the variance of estimation integrated over the entire input space, as a criterion for sampling new data points. However, such an integration treats each input point equally and does not account for their different output values. This is far from ideal for applications such as extreme event estimation [58], where one would like to estimate the mapping accurately for inputs whose outputs occur with small probabilities. Therefore, [70] proposed to weight each variance in the integration by the inverse of its output probability. The resulting acquisition function can also be interpreted as an approximation to the $l_{1}$ -difference between the true mapping and the estimated mapping (see Section 4 in their paper).

Translating this to the optimal intervention design problem considered in our work, the output can be taken to be the optimality gap of the input interventions. Our goal is to optimize this output value, which depends non-linearly on the input. Towards this end, a stronger objective is to estimate the output value accurately over the entire input space. This results in the CIV acquisition function described in the main text, which uses a uniform measure $\nu$ on $\mathcal{A}$ . We can further improve this by putting more importance on inputs that result in better output values. To achieve this, we make use of the output weighting scheme in [70].

### C.2 Output-weight Calculations

Let $f_{{\mathbf{a}}}$ be the probability density function (pdf) of a uniform distribution on the input space $\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ . This induces a distribution on the optimality gap with pdf $f_{\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}}$ . Recall that ${\mathbf{b}}=({\mathbf{I}}-\mathbb{E}({\mathbf{B}}|\mathcal{D}_{t})){\bm{\mu}}^{*}$ is the estimated optimal intervention based on $\mathcal{D}_{t}$ . The output-weighted method uses the measure

$$ d\nu({\mathbf{a}})=\frac{f_{\mathbf{a}}({\mathbf{a}})}{f_{\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}}(\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2})}d{\mathbf{a}}. $$

Using the formula for the area of the hyperspherical cap, we can calculate this ratio explicitly as follows.

#### Lemma 4.

For any ${\mathbf{a}}\in\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ , it holds that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{f_{\mathbf{a}}({\mathbf{a}})}{f_{\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}}(\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2})}\propto\left(\frac{1}{\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-({\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}})^{2}}\right)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $f_{\mathbf{a}}$ is the pdf of the uniform distribution on $\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ , it holds that

$$ \displaystyle f_{\mathbf{a}}({\mathbf{a}})\propto 1. $$

As illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 1, the induced probability $\mathbb{P}(\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq k)$ corresponds to the probability of ${\mathbf{a}}$ being on the hyperspherical cap with angle $\phi$ satisfying

$$ \cos\phi=\frac{1+\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-k}{2\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}}. $$

*Supplementary Figure 1: Schematic illustrating the calculation of output-weighting. Hyperspherical cap corresponding to $\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq k$ with angle $\phi$ .*

Using the formula for the area of the hyperspherical cap [53], we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}(\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq k)\propto\int_{0}^{1-\cos^{2}\phi}u^{\frac{p-3}{2}}(1-u)^{-\frac{1}{2}}du. $$

Thus, using the Leibniz integral rule, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle f_{\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}}(\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}=k) \displaystyle\propto\frac{\partial\mathbb{P}(\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq k)}{\partial k} \displaystyle=(1-\cos^{2}\phi)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}(\cos\phi)^{-1}\frac{\partial(1-\cos^{2}\phi)}{\partial k} \displaystyle=(1+\cos\phi)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}(1-\cos\phi)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}(\cos\phi)^{-1}\frac{\partial(1-\cos^{2}\phi)}{\partial k} \displaystyle=\left(\left(1+\frac{1+\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-k}{2\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}}\right)\left(1-\frac{1+\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-k}{2\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}}\right)\right)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}\cdot\frac{1}{\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}}\left(\frac{\big((1+\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2})^{2}-k\big)\big(-(1-\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2})^{2}+k\big)}{4\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}}\right)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}. $$

As a consequence, we obtain that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{f_{\mathbf{a}}({\mathbf{a}})}{f_{\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}}(\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2})} \displaystyle\propto\left(\frac{1}{\big((1+\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2})^{2}-\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}\big)\big(-(1-\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2})^{2}+\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}\big)}\right)^{\frac{p-3}{2}} \displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{(2\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}+2{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}})(2\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}-2{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}})}\right)^{\frac{p-3}{2}} \displaystyle\propto\left(\frac{1}{\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-({\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}})^{2}}\right)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}, $$

where we used $\|{\mathbf{a}}\|_{2}=1$ in the second line. This completes the proof. ∎

#### Remark 4.

Note that based on this formula, the resulting weighting scheme is symmetric, in the sense that $d\nu({\mathbf{a}})=d\nu(-{\mathbf{a}})$ for any ${\mathbf{a}}\in\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ . Therefore when up-weighting ${\mathbf{a}}$ ’s that are close to ${\mathbf{a}}^{*}$ , we also up-weight ${\mathbf{a}}$ ’s that are close to $-{\mathbf{a}}^{*}$ . Since the optimal intervention can be obtained by minimizing or maximizing $\|{\mathbf{a}}-{\mathbf{a}}^{*}\|_{2}^{2}$ , a reasonable choice is to up-weight ${\mathbf{a}}$ ’s that are close to its extremum. The symmetric weighting scheme adopted here achieves this.

When $p>3$ , this measure puts more weight on ${\mathbf{a}}\in\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ with larger $|{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}}|$ , i.e., directions that are more aligned with the estimated optimal intervention ${\mathbf{b}}$ . However, when $p=3$ , this measure degenerates to the uniform measure on $\mathcal{A}$ . To obtain the desired behavior when $p=3$ , we instead propose using the bimodal von-Mises Fisher distribution

$$ \displaystyle d\nu({\mathbf{a}})=\left(e^{\kappa{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}}}+e^{-\kappa{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}}}\right)d{\mathbf{a}}, $$

with a suitable scale $\kappa>0$ . Note that this measure discounts ${\mathbf{a}}$ exponentially with the value of $|{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}}|$ , and therefore behaves similar to the output-weighted measure in high dimensions.

### C.3 Approximation of CIV-OW

We now show how to evaluate the causal output-weighted integrated variance (CIV-OW) acquisition function

$$ \displaystyle h_{\mathrm{OW}}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})=\int_{\mathcal{A}}\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})}d\nu({\mathbf{a}}), $$

where using Lemma 4 and Remark 4,

$$ \displaystyle d\nu({\mathbf{a}})\propto\begin{cases}\left(\frac{1}{\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-({\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}})^{2}}\right)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}d{\mathbf{a}},&p>3\\
\left(e^{\kappa{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}}}+e^{-\kappa{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}}}\right)d{\mathbf{a}},&p=3.\end{cases} $$

In the case when $p=2$ , there are only two variables and it is easy to show that the CIV acquisition function always selects the intervention that targets just the upstream variable, no matter what the measure $\nu$ is. Therefore, we do not need to consider the case $p=2$ .

To evaluate CIV-OW for a particular ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ , first, recall that using Proposition 1., we have

$$ h_{\mathrm{OW}}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})=\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}\left(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i}\right)+4u_{i}\int_{\mathcal{A}}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})\right]+C, $$

where $C$ is a constant that does not depend on ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ . For $p=3$ , we use the first and second moments of the bimodal von-Mises Fisher distribution (see Corollary 2 in [36]) to derive that

$$ \int_{\mathcal{A}}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})=\left(\frac{\coth{\kappa}}{\kappa}-\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}}\right)+\left(2-\frac{3\coth{\kappa}}{\kappa}+\frac{3}{\kappa^{2}}\right)b_{i}^{2}. $$

For $p>3$ , we use the following approximation for the integral:

$$ \int_{\mathcal{A}}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})\approx(1+\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2})\frac{(\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-b_{i}^{2})^{\frac{4-p}{2}}b_{i}^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{p}(\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-b_{j}^{2})^{\frac{4-p}{2}}b_{j}^{2}}. $$

This approximation is obtained as follows: First, note that

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{p}\int_{\mathcal{A}}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}}) \displaystyle=\int_{\mathcal{A}}(\|{\mathbf{a}}\|_{2}^{2}+\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-2{\mathbf{a}}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}})d\nu({\mathbf{a}}) \displaystyle=1+\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}, $$

where we used the symmetry of $\mathcal{A}$ and $\nu({\mathbf{a}})=\nu(-{\mathbf{a}})$ to derive $\int_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathbf{a}}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})=\mathbf{0}$ in the second equation. To obtain only one of the terms in the summation instead of the sum over all possible $i\in[p]$ , it is sufficient to identify the ratio of the integration between two summands $i,j\in[p]$ . We obtain this ratio using the following approximation:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\int_{\mathcal{A}}(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})}{\int_{\mathcal{A}}(a_{j}-b_{j})^{2}d\nu({\mathbf{a}})}\approx\frac{c_{i}}{c_{j}}: \displaystyle=\frac{b_{i}^{2}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-2}(\sqrt{1-b_{i}^{2}/\|{\mathbf{b}}\|^{2}})}\left(\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-i}\|_{2}^{2}-({\mathbf{a}}_{-i}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}}_{-i})^{2}\right)^{\frac{3-p}{2}}d{\mathbf{a}}_{-i}}{b_{j}^{2}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-2}(\sqrt{1-b_{j}^{2}/\|{\mathbf{b}}\|^{2}_{2}})}\left(\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-j}\|_{2}^{2}-({\mathbf{a}}_{-j}^{\top}{\mathbf{b}}_{-j})^{2}\right)^{\frac{3-p}{2}}d{\mathbf{a}}_{-j}} \displaystyle=\frac{b_{i}^{2}\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-i}\|_{2}^{4-p}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-2}(1)}\left(\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-i}\|^{2}a_{1}^{2}\right)^{\frac{3-p}{2}}d{\mathbf{a}}}{b_{j}^{2}\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-j}\|_{2}^{4-p}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{p-2}(1)}\left(\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-j}\|^{2}a_{1}^{2}\right)^{\frac{3-p}{2}}d{\mathbf{a}}} \displaystyle=\frac{b_{i}^{2}\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-i}\|_{2}^{4-p}\int_{-1}^{1}\left(\frac{1-a_{1}^{2}}{b_{i}^{2}+\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-i}\|^{2}(1-a_{1}^{2})}\right)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}da_{1}}{b_{j}^{2}\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-j}\|_{2}^{4-p}\int_{-1}^{1}\left(\frac{1-a_{1}^{2}}{b_{j}^{2}+\|{\mathbf{b}}_{-j}\|^{2}(1-a_{1}^{2})}\right)^{\frac{p-3}{2}}da_{1}}\approx\frac{b_{i}^{2}\big(\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-b_{i}^{2}\big)^{\frac{4-p}{2}}}{b_{j}^{2}\big(\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-b_{j}^{2}\big)^{\frac{4-p}{2}}}, $$

where in the third line we used a change of variables using the area element. The intuition behind the first approximation is that $\nu({\mathbf{a}})$ is exponentially smaller when $|a_{i}|\neq|b_{i}|$ in high dimensions with large $p$ and therefore we can approximate the integration around $|a_{i}|=|b_{i}|$ . Since $(a_{i}-b_{i})^{2}=0$ , this is then contracted to $a_{i}=-b_{i}$ for which we calculate the ratio $\frac{c_{i}}{c_{j}}$ . In the second approximation, we approximated the integration with a constant regardless of $i$ . The intuition for this is that when $p$ grows, the integration will be dominated by $a_{1}=0$ , where the integrated terms for all $i$ are the same.

Combining the sum and ratio formulas in Eq. (37) and Eq. (38) gives rise to the approximation in Eq. (36). We also verified this approximation numerically; see Supplementary Fig. 2. Finally, using Eq. (35) and Eq. (36) in Eq. (34), we can evaluate (approximately when $p>3$ ) CIV-OW for any given ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ in closed form as follows:

$$ \displaystyle h_{\mathrm{OW}}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle\approx \displaystyle\begin{cases}\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i})+\frac{4u_{i}(1+\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2})(\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-b_{i}^{2})^{\frac{4-p}{2}}b_{i}^{2}}{\sum_{j=1}^{p}(\|{\mathbf{b}}\|_{2}^{2}-b_{j}^{2})^{\frac{4-p}{2}}b_{j}^{2}}\right]+C,&p>3\\
\sum_{i=1}^{p}\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}}{\alpha_{i}^{\prime}-1}\left[\frac{\beta_{i}^{\prime}(2\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)}{(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-1)(\alpha^{\prime}_{i}-2)}(u_{i}^{2}+\frac{2}{n}u_{i})+4u_{i}\big((\frac{\coth{\kappa}}{\kappa}-\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}})+(2-\frac{3\coth{\kappa}}{\kappa}+\frac{3}{\kappa^{2}})b_{i}^{2}\big)\right]+C,&p=3.\end{cases}. $$

This then allows for similar optimization methods as described in Sec. B.2 to be used for selecting ${\mathbf{a}}^{(t+1)}$ . The computational complexity of evaluating CIV-OW for a single ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ is $O(p^{3})$ .

## Appendix D Extensions to the Unknown DAG Setting

So far, we have assumed that the underlying causal structure is known and represented by a DAG. In the case of an unknown DAG, we also need to take into account the uncertainty over the DAG structure. We can model this uncertainty over the DAG $\mathcal{G}$ when computing the conditional variance $\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})\mid\mathcal{D}_{t}}$ that is used to compute the causal integrated variance $h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ . In particular, we can add to our generative model a prior $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G})$ over DAGs, and use the DAG-BLR prior conditional on the DAG $\mathcal{G}$ .

To update the posterior on the causal structure along with the causal mechanisms (i.e., the edge weights), we can use the interventional Bayesian equivalance (iBGe) score [32, 47] as follows. Denoting the collection of samples by $\mathcal{D}$ for simplicity, then the joint posterior of the unknown DAG $\mathcal{G}$ , the edge weights ${\mathbf{B}}$ and noise variances ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ satisfy

$$ \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G},{\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{D})=\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}|\mathcal{D}). $$

To select the next intervention based on the CIV acquisition functions, we need to integrate the uncertainty $\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}}$ , where $g({\mathbf{a}})$ only depends on the joint posterior of ${\mathbf{B}}$ and ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ . Marginalizing over $\mathcal{G}$ , we obtain that $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{D})=\sum_{\mathcal{G}}\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}|\mathcal{D})$ . Following [4], we can approximate this posterior by sampling several DAGs $\mathcal{G}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{G}_{k}$ from the iBGe score $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}|\mathcal{D})$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},\Sigma|\mathcal{D})\approx\sum_{l=1}^{k}\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{B}},{\bm{\Sigma}}|\mathcal{G}_{l},\mathcal{D})\cdot\omega(\mathcal{G}_{l}), $$

where $\omega(\mathcal{G}_{l})=\frac{\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}_{l}|\mathcal{D})}{\sum_{l^{\prime}=1}^{k}\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}_{l^{\prime}}|\mathcal{D})}$ is the importance weight for the $l$ -th sampled DAG $\mathcal{G}_{l}$ . We can approximate the uncertainty using an unbiased estimator of its lower bound:

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}} \displaystyle=\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{G}}\big(\mathbb{E}(g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})|\mathcal{D}\big)+\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}\big(\mathrm{Var}(g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})|\mathcal{D}\big) \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{G}}\big(\mathrm{Var}(g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{G},\mathcal{D})|\mathcal{D}\big) \displaystyle\approx\sum_{l=1}^{k}\mathrm{Var}(g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{G}_{l},\mathcal{D})\cdot\omega(\mathcal{G}_{l}). $$

For this, we used the law of total variance in the first equation and then dropped the variance over $\mathcal{G}$ since it is usually intractable. Based on this approximation, we can then approximate the CIV acquisition function as follows:

$$ \displaystyle h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}) \displaystyle\approx\sum_{l=1}^{k}\int_{{\mathbf{a}}}\mathrm{Var}\big(g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{G}_{l},\mathcal{D}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})\big)\cdot\omega(\mathcal{G}_{l})d{\mathbf{a}} \displaystyle=\sum_{l=1}^{k}h({\mathbf{a}},\mathcal{D}_{t}|\mathcal{G}_{l})\cdot\omega(\mathcal{G}_{l}), $$

where $h({\mathbf{a}},\mathcal{D}_{t}|\mathcal{G}_{l})$ can be evaluated as described in Sec. B for any given DAG $\mathcal{G}_{l}$ . This procedure allows the CIV acquisition function to be optimized even in the unknown DAG case. Of note, since the number of DAGs grows super-exponentially with the graph size $p$ , the computational budget is often not sufficient to obtain a large enough sample size $k$ to guarantee accurate approximation. Therefore in practice, one often uses just one DAG, for example the one obtained by maximizing the likelihood of or sampling from $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}|\mathcal{D})$ ; see [4]. We note that sampling DAGs from $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{G}|\mathcal{D})$ is a difficult problem and is considered an open research direction on its own (c.f. [91]).

## Appendix E Proofs for the Mutual Information Bound

To prove Theorem 1 in the main text, we need several lemmas. The following lemma shows that the mutual information between a Gaussian and a non-Gaussian variable can be lower bounded by transforming the non-Gaussian variable into a Gaussian variable. For completeness we provide our proof here and note that alternative proofs exist, for example by using information geometric techniques as in [17].

#### Lemma 5.

Let $\mathsf{x}_{g}$ be a multivariate Gaussian variable following $\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\mathsf{x}_{g}},\Sigma_{\mathsf{x}_{g}})$ , and let $\mathsf{z}$ be an arbitrary univariate random variable with mean $\mu_{\mathsf{z}}$ and variance $\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{2}$ . Denoting by $\rho=\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{-1}\Sigma_{\mathsf{x}_{g}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}((x_{g}-\mu_{\mathsf{x}_{g}})(z-\mu_{\mathsf{z}}))$ and $\mathsf{z}_{g}=\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}\rho^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathsf{x}_{g}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}(\mathsf{x}_{g}-\mu_{\mathsf{x}_{g}})+\mathcal{N}\big(\mu_{\mathsf{z}},(1-\|\rho\|_{2}^{2})\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{2}\big)$ , then

$$ I(\mathsf{z};\mathsf{x}_{g})\geq I(\mathsf{z}_{g};\mathsf{x}_{g}). $$

#### Remark 5.

Note that here $\mathsf{z}_{g}$ can be understood as a transformation of $\mathsf{z}$ to a linear combination of $\mathsf{x}_{g}$ and some independent Gaussian noise. The choices of the linear coefficients are to make sure that i) the correlation between $\mathsf{z}_{g}$ and $\mathsf{x}$ is kept the same as that between $\mathsf{z}$ and $\mathsf{x}$ ; ii) $\mathsf{z}_{g}$ has the same mean and variance as $\mathsf{z}$ . The reason for these two requirements will become evident in the proof.

#### Proof of Lemma 5.

First, note that

$$ \displaystyle I(\mathsf{z};\mathsf{x}_{g}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}(x_{g},z)}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}}(x_{g})\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{z}}(z)}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}}(x_{g}|z)}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}_{g}}(x_{g}|z)}\right)+\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}_{g}}(x_{g}|z)}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}}(x_{g})}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{z}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}}(x_{g}|z)}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}_{g}}(x_{g}|z)}\right)+\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}_{g}}(x_{g}|z)}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}}(x_{g})}\right) \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}_{g}}(x_{g}|z)}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}}(x_{g})}\right)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|\mathsf{x}_{g}}(z|x_{g})}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{z}_{g}}(z)}\right), $$

where $\log=\log_{2}$ and we used the Gibb’s inequality $\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}}(x_{g}|z)}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{x}_{g}|\mathsf{z}_{g}}(x_{g}|z)}\right)\geq 0$ in the fourth line. Since $\mathsf{z}_{g}$ is a Gaussian variable with mean and variance

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{\mathsf{z}_{g}} \displaystyle=\mu_{\mathsf{z}}, \displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}_{g}} \displaystyle=\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}}, $$

conditioning on $\mathsf{x}_{g}=x_{g}$ results in a Gaussian variable with mean and variance

$$ \displaystyle\mu_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|x_{g}} \displaystyle=\mu_{\mathsf{z}}+\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}\rho^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathsf{x}_{g}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}(x_{g}-\mu_{\mathsf{x}_{g}}), \displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|x_{g}} \displaystyle=(1-\|\rho\|^{2}_{2})\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}}. $$

Therefore, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle I(\mathsf{z};\mathsf{x}_{g}) \displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|\mathsf{x}_{g}}(z|x_{g})}{\mathbb{P}_{\mathsf{z}_{g}}(z)}\right) \displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\left(\log\frac{\sigma_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|x_{g}}^{-1}\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2\sigma_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|x_{g}}^{2}}(z-\mu_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|x_{g}})^{2}\right)}{\sigma_{\mathsf{z}_{g}}^{-1}\exp\big(-\frac{1}{2\sigma_{\mathsf{z}_{g}}^{2}}(z-\mu_{\mathsf{z}_{g}})^{2}\big)}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1}{1-\|\rho\|^{2}_{2}}+\frac{\log e}{2}\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\left(\frac{(z-\mu_{\mathsf{z}_{g}})^{2}}{\sigma_{\mathsf{z}_{g}}^{2}}-\frac{(z-\mu_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|x_{g}})^{2}}{\sigma_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|x_{g}}^{2}}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1}{1-\|\rho\|^{2}_{2}}+\frac{\log e}{2}\left(\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{z}}(z-\mu_{\mathsf{z}_{g}})^{2}}{\sigma_{\mathsf{z}_{g}}^{2}}-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}(z-\mu_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|x_{g}})^{2}}{\sigma_{\mathsf{z}_{g}|x_{g}}^{2}}\right) $$

where we used Eq. (40) and Eq. (41) for the last equation. As a consequence,

$$ \displaystyle I(\mathsf{z};\mathsf{x}_{g}) \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1}{1-\|\rho\|^{2}_{2}}+\frac{\log e}{2}\left(\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{z}}(z-\mu_{\mathsf{z}})^{2}}{\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{2}}-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}_{g},\mathsf{z}}\big((z-\mu_{\mathsf{z}})-\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}\rho^{\top}\Sigma_{\mathsf{x}_{g}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}(x_{g}-\mu_{\mathsf{x}_{g}})\big)^{2}}{(1-\|\rho\|^{2}_{2})\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{2}}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1}{1-\|\rho\|^{2}_{2}}+\frac{\log e}{2}\left(1-\frac{\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{2}+\|\rho\|^{2}_{2}\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{2}-2\|\rho\|^{2}_{2}\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{2}}{(1-\|\rho\|^{2}_{2})\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{2}}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1}{1-\|\rho\|^{2}_{2}}=I(\mathsf{z}_{g};\mathsf{x}_{g}), $$

which completes the proof. ∎

Next, we derive an equation for the correlation between two random variables. Since the mutual information between two Gaussian random variables is a function of their correlation, we can then use the following lemma to get another expression of the mutual information. Note that in the following, we use $\sigma^{2}_{\cdot}$ to denote the variance of a scalar random variable, e.g., $\sigma_{\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}=x}^{2}=\mathrm{Var}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}=x)$ denotes the variance of the scalar variable $\mathsf{z}$ following the conditional distribution $\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}=x)$ .

#### Lemma 6.

Let $\mathsf{x}$ and $\mathsf{z}$ be random variables such that $\mathsf{x}$ is multivariate and $\mathsf{z}$ is univariate. For any multivariate $\mathsf{x}^{\prime}$ and univariate $\mathsf{z}^{\prime}$ , we define $\rho_{\mathsf{x}^{\prime},\mathsf{z}^{\prime}}:=\sigma_{\mathsf{z}^{\prime}}^{-1}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathsf{x}^{\prime}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}^{\prime},\mathsf{z}^{\prime}}((x^{\prime}-\mu_{\mathsf{x}^{\prime}})(z^{\prime}-\mu_{\mathsf{z}^{\prime}}))$ . It holds that

$$ \|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z}}\|_{2}^{2}=\left(1-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}}(\sigma_{\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}}^{2})}{\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}}}\right)\|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})}\|_{2}^{2}. $$

#### Proof.

Multiplying both sides of the desired equality (42) by $\sigma_{\mathsf{z}}^{2}$ and expanding $\|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z}}\|_{2}^{2}$ , we obtain that

$$ \displaystyle\|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z}}\|_{2}^{2}=\left(1-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}}(\sigma_{\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}}^{2})}{\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}}}\right)\|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})}\|_{2}^{2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathrm{Cov}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z})^{\top}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathsf{x}}^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z})=(\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}}-\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}}(\sigma_{\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}}^{2}))\cdot\|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})}\|_{2}^{2}. $$

Thus, it suffices to show that $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z})^{\top}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathsf{x}}^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z})=(\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}}-\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}}(\sigma_{\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}}^{2}))\cdot\|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})}\|_{2}^{2}$ . By the law of total expectation,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z})=\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{x}\mathsf{z})-\mathbb{E}\mathsf{x}\cdot\mathbb{E}\mathsf{z}=\mathbb{E}\big(\mathsf{x}\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})\big)-\mathbb{E}\mathsf{x}\cdot\mathbb{E}\big(\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})\big)=\mathrm{Cov}\big(\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})\big), $$

and by the law of total variance,

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}}-\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}}(\sigma_{\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}}^{2}) \displaystyle=\mathrm{Var}(\mathsf{z})-\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}}\big(\mathrm{Var}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}=x)\big) \displaystyle=\mathrm{Var}_{\mathsf{x}}\big(\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}=x)\big)=\sigma^{2}_{\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})}. $$

Therefore, using Eq. (43) and Eq. (44) together with the definition of $\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})}$ results in

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Cov}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z})^{\top}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathsf{x}}^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z}) \displaystyle=\mathrm{Cov}\big(\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})\big)^{\top}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathsf{x}}^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}\big(\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})\big), \displaystyle(\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}}-\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}}(\sigma_{\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}}^{2}))\|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})}\|_{2}^{2} \displaystyle=\mathrm{Cov}\big(\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})\big)^{\top}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathsf{x}}^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}\big(\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})\big), $$

which proves that $\mathrm{Cov}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z})^{\top}{\bm{\Sigma}}_{\mathsf{x}}^{-1}\mathrm{Cov}(\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z})=(\sigma^{2}_{\mathsf{z}}-\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{x}}(\sigma_{\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x}}^{2}))\|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathbb{E}(\mathsf{z}|\mathsf{x})}\|_{2}^{2}$ , as desired. ∎

Next, we show that we can transform a non-Gaussian variable into a Gaussian variable using deterministic functions. This is an extension of Theorem 2 in [63], whose scalar version is proven in [75]. We restate the extended version in the following lemma and provide a proof here.

#### Lemma 7.

Let $\mathsf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ be a multivariate random variable following a distribution with continuous and strictly increasing conditional cumulative distribution functions (cdf) $F_{\mathsf{x}_{1}},F_{\mathsf{x}_{2}|\mathsf{x}_{1}},...,F_{\mathsf{x}_{p}|\mathsf{x}_{1:p-1}}$ , where $\mathsf{x}_{1:p-1}$ denotes the collection of $\mathsf{x}_{1},\mathsf{x}_{2},...,\mathsf{x}_{p-1}$ . Let $\Phi_{N}^{-1}$ be the inverse cdf of $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ . Then the transformation $\mathsf{u}=\Phi(\mathsf{x})$ defined by

$$ \displaystyle\mathsf{u}_{1} \displaystyle=\Phi^{-1}_{N}\cdot F_{\mathsf{x}_{1}}(\mathsf{x}_{1}), \displaystyle\mathsf{u}_{2}|u_{1} \displaystyle=\Phi^{-1}_{N}\cdot F_{\mathsf{x}_{2}|\mathsf{u}_{1}}(\mathsf{x}_{2}|\mathsf{u}_{1}=u_{1}), \displaystyle... \displaystyle\mathsf{u}_{2}|u_{1:p-1} \displaystyle=\Phi^{-1}_{N}\cdot F_{\mathsf{x}_{p}|\mathsf{u}_{1:p}}(\mathsf{x}_{p}|\mathsf{u}_{1:p-1}=u_{1:p-1}) $$

is invertible and $\mathsf{u}\sim\mathcal{N}({\bm{0}},{\mathbf{I}})$ .

#### Proof.

First note that the cdf of $\mathsf{u}_{1}$ satisfies $F_{\mathsf{u}_{1}}(u)=\mathbb{P}(\Phi_{N}^{-1}\cdot F_{\mathsf{x}_{1}}(\mathsf{x}_{1})\leq u)=\mathbb{P}(F_{\mathsf{x}_{1}}(\mathsf{x}_{1})\leq\Phi_{N}(u))=\Phi_{N}(u)$ , and therefore $\mathsf{u}_{1}$ is $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ -distributed. Similar arguments can be used to show that each of $\mathsf{u}_{2}|u_{1},\dots,\mathsf{u}_{p}|u_{1:p-1}$ is $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ -distributed. Therefore, the joint distribution $\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{u}_{1:p})=\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{u}_{1})\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{u}_{2}|\mathsf{u}_{1})\dots$ $\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{u}_{p}|\mathsf{u}_{1:p-1})=\mathcal{N}(0,1)^{p}$ is a multivariate Gaussian $\mathcal{N}({\bm{0}},{\mathbf{I}})$ .

Second, since $F_{\mathsf{x}_{1}}$ is continuous and strictly increasing, the transformation $\mathsf{x}_{1}\rightarrow\mathsf{u}_{1}$ is invertible and continuous. This, together with the fact that $F_{\mathsf{x}_{2}|\mathsf{x}_{1}}$ is continuous and strictly increasing, means that $F_{\mathsf{x}_{2}|\mathsf{u}_{1}}$ is continuous and strictly increasing. Therefore $\mathsf{x}_{1},\mathsf{x}_{2}\rightarrow\mathsf{u}_{1},\mathsf{u}_{2}$ is invertible and continuous. By iterating this argument it follows that the transformation $\mathsf{x}_{1},...,\mathsf{x}_{p}\rightarrow\mathsf{u}_{1},...,\mathsf{u}_{p}$ , i.e., $\Phi$ , is invertible, which completes the proof. ∎

With these results, we can now prove Theorem 1 from the main text. We first use Lemma 7 to transform the sample distribution into a Gaussian distribution. Then we derive a lower bound on the mutual information using Lemma 5. This lower bound is simplified to be a scalar multiplied by the relative decay, using Lemma 6.

#### Proof of Theorem 1.

Let $\Phi$ be the transformation in Lemma 7 that turns the random variable $\mathsf{x}^{\prime}\sim\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}^{\prime}|\mathcal{D}_{t},{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ into a Gaussian variable $\Phi(\mathsf{x}^{\prime})\sim\mathcal{N}({\bm{0}},{\mathbf{I}})$ . Here, the distribution before the transformation is $\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}^{\prime}|\mathcal{D}_{t},{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})=\mathbb{P}(({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}})^{-1}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}+{\bm{\epsilon}}^{\prime})|\mathcal{D}_{t})$ , the posterior of sample ${\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}$ from ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}$ given data $\mathcal{D}_{t}$ . This posterior can be viewed as an induced distribution of $({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}})^{-1}({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}+{\bm{\epsilon}}^{\prime})$ , where ${\mathbf{B}}$ and ${\bm{\epsilon}}^{\prime}$ follow the posteriors given $\mathcal{D}_{t}$ obtained in Lemma 1. Let $\mathcal{E}=\{\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{x}^{\prime}|\mathcal{D}_{t},{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}):{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}\}$ denote the class of all such posterior distributions.

Using the data processing inequality it holds that

$$ I(g({\mathbf{a}});{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})\geq I(g({\mathbf{a}});\Phi({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t}). $$

Now since $\Phi({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})$ is multivariate Gaussian, we can use Lemma 5 to derive that

$$ \displaystyle I(g({\mathbf{a}});{\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle\geq I(g({\mathbf{a}});\Phi({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t}) \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}\log\frac{1}{1-\|\rho_{\Phi({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}),g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t}}\|_{2}^{2}}\geq\frac{1}{2}\|\rho_{\Phi({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}),g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t}}\|_{2}^{2}, $$

where we denote $\rho_{\Phi({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}),g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t}}=\sigma_{g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}}^{-1}\mathrm{Var}(\Phi({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime})|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathrm{Cov}(\Phi({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}),g({\mathbf{a}})|{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ . Next, we apply Lemma 6 to obtain

where $\rho$ only depends on $\mathcal{D}_{t}$ , the family of posterior distributions $\mathcal{E}$ , and the function of interest $g$ . This completes the proof. ∎

#### Remark 6 (Evaluation of $\rho$ ).

We note that since $\|\rho_{\mathsf{x},\mathsf{z}}\|_{2}^{2}\leq 1$ for any multivariate $\mathsf{x}$ and univariate $\mathsf{z}$ , it holds that $\rho^{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}$ in the proof of Theorem 1 above. While Theorem 1 applies to general posterior modeling of an intervention effect $\mathbb{P}({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}|\mathcal{D}_{t},{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime})$ and variable of interest $\mathbb{P}(g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}\cup({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))$ , for certain special cases we can compute the constant $\rho^{2}$ exactly. In particular, in the following we show that $\rho^{2}=\frac{1}{2}$ for the prominent special case of Bayesian linear regression, also considered in [70].

In the Bayesian linear regression setting, the “intervention effect” $\mathbb{P}(\mathsf{y}|\mathcal{D},\mathsf{x})$ corresponds to the output distribution of $\mathsf{y}$ given input $\mathsf{x}$ and previous data $\mathcal{D}$ , which is modeled as $\mathsf{y}=\theta^{\top}\mathsf{x}$ with $\theta$ following a Gaussian posterior. The “variable of interest” is any linear transformation of $\theta$ , e.g., $c^{\top}\theta$ for some constant vector $c$ . Then $\Phi$ is a linear transformation of $\mathsf{y}$ , and $\mathbb{E}(c^{\top}\theta|\mathcal{D}\cup({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))$ is linear in $\mathsf{y}$ . Therefore $\rho^{2}(c^{\top}\theta;\mathsf{y}|\mathsf{x},\mathcal{D})$ , written out similarly as in Eq. (48), equals $\nicefrac{{c}}{{\|c\|_{2}}}$ for all input $\mathsf{x}$ . Thus $\rho^{2}$ in Theorem 1 equals exactly $\frac{1}{2}$ , and as a consequence,

$$ I(c^{\top}\theta;\mathsf{y}|\mathsf{x},\mathcal{D})\geq\frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathsf{y}}\left(\sigma^{2}_{c^{\top}\theta|\mathcal{D}\cup(\mathsf{y},\mathsf{x})}\right)}{\sigma^{2}_{c^{\top}\theta|\mathcal{D}}}\right) $$

For the case of a linear SCM with a DAG-Wishart prior, however, direct calculation of $\rho^{2}$ can be difficult since (i) the posterior distribution of ${\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}$ is a composition of two normal-Wishart distributions, and (ii) $\mathbb{E}(g({\mathbf{a}})|\mathcal{D}_{t}\cup({\mathbf{x}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}))$ is a complicated function of ${\mathbf{x}}^{\prime}$ , given in Proposition 1.. Of note, $\rho^{2}$ can be made larger by considering transformations $\Phi$ beyond Lemma 7, which is related to research on Gaussianization [63].

#### Remark 7.

We make a note about the case where $h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ degenerates to constant $0$ for all ${\mathbf{a}}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}$ . From the proof above, we see that this is equivalent to the case where ${\bm{\mu}}^{*}_{\pa(i)}={\mathbf{A}}_{i}{\mathbf{a}}^{*}={\bm{0}}$ for all $i\in[p]$ . This is also equivalent to the optimal intervention ${\mathbf{a}}^{*}$ only intervenes on sink nodes, i.e., nodes with no children. For such ${\mathbf{a}}^{*}$ , we can directly calculate ${\mathbf{a}}^{*}$ by subtracting the target and source distribution, ${\mathbf{a}}^{*}=({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}}){\bm{\mu}}^{*}={\bm{\mu}}^{*}$ , since ${\mathbf{B}}{\bm{\mu}}^{*}={\bm{0}}$ . Therefore, in simulations, we avoid this case and generate ${\mathbf{a}}^{*}$ that targets not only the sink nodes.

This theorem implies that ${\mathbf{a}}^{*}$ is an approximate- $O(\nicefrac{{1}}{{t^{2}}})$ local minimum of $h({\mathbf{a}}^{\prime},\mathcal{D}_{t})$ . Note that here we define the approximate local minima following [2, 62], where the asymptotic notation means that there exists a constant $c\geq 0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\|\nabla h({\mathbf{a}}^{*},\mathcal{D}_{t})\|\leq\frac{c^{2}}{t^{2}}\quad and\quad\nabla^{2}h({\mathbf{a}}^{*},\mathcal{D}_{t})\succeq-\frac{c}{t}{\mathbf{I}}. $$

Note, however, that approximate local minima are not guaranteed to be closed to any local minimum unless additional constraints are satisfied by the function [2].

## Appendix G Extended Simulation Results

In this section, we provide a detailed description of the simulated dataset and present additional empirical results.

To construct a synthetic instance of a causal system and an optimal intervention, we use the following procedure:

- (i) Generate a DAG $\mathcal{G}$ with $p$ nodes. Specifically, in our experiments $p$ ranges from $10$ to $30$ . To analyze the effect of edge density on our results, we consider different types of graphs including complete graphs, Erdös-Rényi graphs [27], and path graphs. The edges in the graph are oriented to obtain a DAG by uniformly sampling a permutation of the nodes and orienting the edges according to the order given by the permutation. Examples of these three types of graphs on $p=5$ nodes are shown in Supplementary Fig. 3.

- (ii) For each edge $k\rightarrow i$ in $\mathcal{G}$ , its corresponding edge weight ${\mathbf{B}}_{ik}$ is generated by sampling from a uniform distribution bounded away from zero, namely ${\mathbf{B}}_{ik}\sim\mathrm{Unif}[-1,-0.25]\cup[0.25,1]$ .

- (iii) The noise levels ${\bm{\Sigma}}$ are chosen so as to standardize the causal model, i.e., ensure that the variance of each variable $\mathsf{x}_{i}$ for $i\in[p]$ is of the same scale. Such standardization has been shown to be important for benchmarking causal inference algorithms [67], although for the problem considered here we found it to not change the results. We used the standardized model proposed in [59] with $\epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ and then re-scaling the causal mechanism $\mathsf{x}_{i}=\sum_{k=1}^{p}{\mathbf{B}}_{ik}\mathsf{x}_{k}+\epsilon_{i}$ by $\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(\mathsf{x}_{i})}$ . We still denote the re-scaled model as ${\mathbf{x}}={\mathbf{B}}{\mathbf{x}}+{\bm{\epsilon}},{\bm{\epsilon}}\sim\mathcal{N}({\bm{0}},{\bm{\Sigma}})$ in the following.

- (iv) Generate the optimal intervention ${\mathbf{a}}^{*}\in\mathcal{A}$ with a fixed-size support in $[p]$ . Specifically, in our experiments we use the unit hypersphere $\mathbb{S}^{p-1}$ as the feasible set $\mathcal{A}$ and $\|{\mathbf{a}}^{*}\|_{0}$ ranges between $1$ and $\lfloor\nicefrac{{p}}{{2}}\rfloor$ . The target mean ${\bm{\mu}}^{*}=({\mathbf{I}}-{\mathbf{B}})^{-1}{\mathbf{a}}^{*}$ is calculated using the ground truth ${\mathbf{B}}$ .

Only the DAG $\mathcal{G}$ and the target mean ${\bm{\mu}}^{*}$ are revealed to the learner. Then the learner proceeds as indicated in Fig. 1 in the main text, i.e., the learner selects an intervention based on the acquisition function, samples from this intervention are generated using Eq. (2) in the main text, and the model is updated based on Lemma 1..
